Python interop

Source: vignettes/interop.qmd

The process at the other end of a channel does not have to be R. pymizu is the Python counterpart of mizu, built on the same shared-memory core. A channel connects the two languages as directly as two R sessions. Pass the peer program as a source string instead of a quoted expression, and set the launcher to mizu_py_launcher(). The launcher checks for the interpreter and pymizu before the channel is created, then spawns python3 -m pymizu.child. In this example, a Python process doubles the Old Faithful eruption durations. (The Python examples in this vignette run when a python3 with pymizu and NumPy installed is on the PATH.)

library(mizu)

ch <- mizu_channel(
  r"(
import pymizu
while True:
    x = ch.recv(30)
    if pymizu.is_sentinel(x):
        break
    ch.send(x * 2)
)",
  launcher = mizu_py_launcher()
)

mizu_send(ch, faithful$eruptions)
head(mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 5))
#> [1] 7.200 3.600 6.666 4.566 9.066 5.766
mizu_close(ch)

Large data crosses without copying

Past a size floor, the data itself never moves. mizu writes it to shared memory once, and both sides read it in place: no serialization, no parsing, no further copies. A large value you receive arrives as an ALTREP view over the shared pages. This is the same zero-copy mechanism you get from another R process. A large value you send arrives in Python backed by those same pages. The peer below echoes back whatever it receives. This channel stays open for the next few examples:

ch <- mizu_channel(
  r"(
import pymizu
while True:
    x = ch.recv(30)
    if pymizu.is_sentinel(x):
        break
    ch.send(x)
)",
  launcher = mizu_py_launcher()
)

big <- rep(faithful$waiting, 5000) # 1.36 million waiting times, ten megabytes
mizu_send(ch, big)
back <- mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 5)
identical(back, big)
#> [1] TRUE

Apart from that one write into the shared region, nothing moved at all. Python’s echo came back as a reference with zero payload bytes. If you send a received view onward, it crosses the same way: as the region’s name alone. So does an unmodified data frame echoed back. The zero-copy tier covers every large layout: a flat vector, a matrix or array of any memory order, a character vector, or a nested Python tree of lists, dicts, and arrays. A large data frame crosses as one shared region in both directions. The floor is low: 256 KB for a flat vector on a channel, and 32 KB everywhere else.1

What crosses

R’s built-in datasets supply the proof: each form below comes back from Python identical() to what you sent, down to values, shape, class, and labels.

echo <- function(x) {
  mizu_send(ch, x)
  mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 5)
}

identical(echo(mtcars), mtcars)              # a data frame
#> [1] TRUE
identical(echo(iris), iris)                  # a factor column stays a factor
#> [1] TRUE
identical(echo(state.x77), state.x77)        # a matrix keeps its dimnames
#> [1] TRUE
identical(echo(HairEyeColor), HairEyeColor)  # a table keeps class and axis labels
#> [1] TRUE
identical(echo(islands), islands)            # a named vector keeps its names
#> [1] TRUE
identical(echo(esoph), esoph)                # ordered factors keep levels and order
#> [1] TRUE

days <- as.Date(paste(1973, airquality$Month, airquality$Day, sep = "-"))
identical(echo(days), days)                  # a Date keeps its meaning
#> [1] TRUE

Python sees the natural equivalent throughout: a NumPy array for a vector, a dict for a named list, a datetime64 array for a Date, a pymizu.Frame for a data frame.

What doesn’t cross

Some values have no portable home on the other side. mizu_send() declines these with a mizu_error_not_portable that points at the offending value. The channel stays usable. Among the built-in datasets, CO2 and ChickWeight cross once their groupedData metadata is dropped: the formula attributes are language objects, and units is a reserved attribute name (the frames and their ordered-factor columns cross fine, and the labels extra rides along).

tryCatch(mizu_send(ch, CO2), error = conditionMessage)
#> [1] "mizu: value is not portable to the peer (an attribute set (formula, outer, labels) outside the portable whitelist at x)"
mizu_close(ch)

mizu_send() also declines a POSIXlt time, a character matrix, an S4 object, a data.table, and a named character vector or named factor (names ride on the plain atomic vectors only). From the Python side, the declined types are nested, decimal, date64, time, and interval Arrow columns.

Data frames and Arrow

A data frame crosses as a pymizu.Frame, one pl.from_arrow(f) or pa.table(f) away from polars or pyarrow. A polars, pyarrow, or pandas frame arrives back as a data.frame. A tibble’s class and extra attributes cross unchanged. An unmodified round trip is identical(): a tibble comes back a tibble.

Any Arrow producer stages directly from its buffers: an arrow Table or RecordBatchReader, a struct-typed nanoarrow_array_stream, DBI::dbGetQueryArrow(), duckdb, or adbc. Staging is one layout write into the shared region, not a conversion to R values first. mizu_as_arrow() converts a received frame back to Arrow. Columns without attributes (double, integer, integer64, character) convert without copying:

ch <- mizu_channel(quote(mizu_send(ch, mizu_recv(ch))))
mizu_send(ch, arrow::arrow_table(data.frame(
  eruptions = rep(faithful$eruptions, 500),
  waiting = rep(faithful$waiting, 500)
)))

df <- mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 30)
arrow::as_arrow_table(mizu_as_arrow(df))
#> Table
#> 136000 rows x 2 columns
#> $eruptions <double>
#> $waiting <double>

# a subset keeps the same backing pages
arrow::as_arrow_table(mizu_as_arrow(df["waiting"]))
#> Table
#> 136000 rows x 1 columns
#> $waiting <double>
mizu_close(ch)

Sending a stream consumes it: a RecordBatchReader is fully materialized at send. The fidelity is frame-level, not Arrow-schema-exact: a dictionary returns as a factor, and unsigned integers widen. The dtype matrix on the pymizu site has the exact per-dtype correspondence.

Mixed-language pools

Channels move values. Pools move computation, and a pool’s workers can be Python processes too. mizu_py_pool_launcher() spawns the workers. mizu_call() builds a language-neutral task: a qualified "mod.fn" name or a .source = string, plus constant arguments. mizu_submit_call() submits it. Unnamed arguments become Python’s positional arguments, and named ones become its keyword arguments:

p <- mizu_pool(2L, launcher = mizu_py_pool_launcher())

t <- mizu_submit_call(p, mizu_call("numpy.quantile", faithful$eruptions, q = c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)))
mizu_collect(t)
#> [1] 2.16275 4.00000 4.45425
quantile(faithful$eruptions, c(0.25, 0.5, 0.75)) # R's own answer, for comparison
#>     25%     50%     75% 
#> 2.16275 4.00000 4.45425

s <- mizu_submit_call(p, mizu_call(.source = "y = x * 2\ny + 1", x = 20))
mizu_collect(s)
#> [1] 41

A .source = task runs in a fresh namespace with the named arguments bound as names. The trailing expression’s value is the result. A plain mizu_submit() on a Python pool fails locally, and the error points to mizu_submit_call(). Task errors cross as mizu_error_remote conditions that keep the remote type. Arguments follow the same rules as channel payloads, zero-copy included. A large array crosses as one shared view, and a view already in shared memory crosses as its name alone. The reverse direction mirrors this: pymizu.Pool.create() with pymizu.r_pool_launcher(), and Pool.submit() with pymizu.call() specs.

The cross-language map

To map a Python function over an R vector, pass a mizu_call() spec as mizu_map()’s .f. Each element of .x becomes the spec’s first positional argument, or binds as x for a .source = spec. .template, .collect = "view", and .seed work as they do on a same-language map:

m <- mizu_map(p, faithful$waiting[1:6], mizu_call("numpy.log"), .template = numeric(1))
mizu_collect(m)
#> [1] 4.369448 3.988984 4.304065 4.127134 4.442651 4.007333
mizu_pool_stop(p)
